sections.title: Optional: an interval for a win rate
paragraphs: Prerequisites: the expectancy and uncertainty sections of this chapter, and comfort with a square root. An observed proportion is an estimate. NIST’s Dataplot documentation gives the Wilson score interval as an alternative to a symmetric normal-approximation interval. Its limits stay within the probability range. The formula used here comes from that documentation; the linked handbook also discusses exact binomial intervals. With p̂ = 12/20 = 0.60, n = 20, and z ≈ 1.96 for 95%, the limits are [p̂ + z²/(2n) ± z × √(p̂(1 − p̂)/n + z²/(4n²))] ÷ (1 + z²/n). Numerically, the center term is 0.60 + 0.09604 = 0.69604, the square-root term is 1.96 × √(0.0120 + 0.002401) ≈ 0.23521, and the divisor is 1.19208. The interval is approximately 38.66% to 78.12%. That range is compatible with materially different trading interpretations.

This interval assumes independent Bernoulli trials with a common probability. Trades across changing regimes or simultaneous stocks may violate those assumptions. It is not a 95% probability guarantee for the next trade, nor a direct interval for expected profit. Win sizes and loss sizes remain unknown even when the win probability is well estimated. A frequentist confidence procedure describes its long-run coverage under its model; the particular observed interval does not assign a probability to a fixed underlying parameter.

sections.title: Optional: dependence reduces the information you have
paragraphs: Prerequisites: the uncertainty section of this chapter. Twenty trades taken during one sector rally may share a driver. Counting each as independent can make the sample look more informative than it is. If Maya’s twenty trades came in four bursts of five, each during a different market episode, the record may behave more like four observations of “how the rule did in that episode” than twenty independent draws, and the standard-error band above would be too narrow. Overlapping holding periods create dependence as well. Inspect results by period, instrument group, and market condition, while remembering that increasingly fine partitions produce small subgroups and additional opportunities to select attractive accidents.

As a brief introduction to a topic needing separate technical study, a bootstrap resamples observed data to study variation in a statistic under a chosen resampling model. For time-dependent returns, block resampling preserves some local sequences rather than shuffling individual days independently. Choosing blocks requires judgment, and a bootstrap cannot manufacture unobserved crises or repair biased data. Treat simulated distributions as conditional on their assumptions. Report whether the result changes materially when a few concentrated observations or one particular period dominate the sample.

sections.title: Optional: annualized return and the Sharpe ratio
paragraphs: Prerequisites: the equity-path section of this chapter, exponents, and the idea of a standard deviation. Compound annual growth rate summarizes start-to-finish compounding: CAGR = (ending equity ÷ starting equity)^(1 ÷ years) − 1, assuming external cash flows have been handled appropriately. If Maya’s twenty paper trades spanned six months, CAGR = (20,605 ÷ 20,000)^(1 ÷ 0.5) − 1 = 1.03025² − 1 ≈ 6.14%. Annualizing expresses the observed growth as an equivalent constant yearly rate. It adds no information and forecasts nothing; projecting that rate forward would assume the observed growth repeats. A short interval can produce a striking annualized number. Report the period and the raw account return beside it.

The Sharpe ratio divides the mean excess, or differential, return by the standard deviation of those same excess returns over a consistent interval. “Excess” requires specifying the reference rate or benchmark. Sharpe shows that multiplying a one-period ratio by the square root of the number of periods relies on zero serial correlation, so multiplying a daily ratio by √252 is a common convention under restrictive assumptions rather than a universally valid step. Dividing Maya’s mean net R by its standard deviation (0.3025 ÷ 1.308 ≈ 0.23) is not a Sharpe ratio: R per trade is not a return over a fixed time interval, and no reference rate has been subtracted. Standard deviation also treats upside and downside variation together and does not directly describe liquidity, leverage, or catastrophic tail exposure. Two methods with similar summary ratios can feel very different to the person holding them.

sections.title: Optional: p-values and how many numbers were considered
paragraphs: Prerequisites: the uncertainty section of this chapter and the variant log in Chapter 24. A p-value is the probability, computed under a specified null model, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed. NIST advises deciding the rejection threshold before seeing the results. A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true (for example, that the rule has no edge), and by itself it says nothing about whether a gross effect survives costs.

Searching changes the interpretation. Maya’s development log in Chapter 24 had six variants. If six independent tests were each run at a 5% threshold on rules with no edge, the chance that at least one passes is 1 − 0.95⁶ ≈ 26%. Variants that share trades are related, which changes that figure, but reporting only the passing variant still overstates the evidence. Bajgrowicz and Scaillet address this at scale, testing 7,846 technical rules on daily Dow Jones Industrial Average data with a false-discovery-rate method; the Research and evidence appendix at the end of the book summarizes what they found. Use each statistic for its own question, then state the uncertainty it leaves unresolved. Apparent precision in a spreadsheet should never conceal fragile definitions, limited independent data, or a large unreported search.

example.title: A payoff ratio is not expectancy
example.text: A planned +2R target and −1R stop give a nominal payoff ratio of 2. If the target occurs only 25% of the time and every other outcome is exactly −1R, gross expectancy is 0.25 × 2 − 0.75 × 1 = −0.25R. The break-even win rate for these two outcomes is 1 ÷ (2 + 1) ≈ 33.3%. Costs raise it, and real trades also include time exits and gaps that a two-outcome picture leaves out.

chapters.exercise: Using the twenty-trade ledger: (a) compute the net win rate, average win, average loss, and expectancy by formula and by direct average, then the gross expectancy; (b) build the equity path from $20,000 at $100 per R and find account return, maximum drawdown in dollars and percent, the gain needed to recover, and the trade at which equity first regains the earlier peak; (c) compute the mean net R without trade 7 and explain why that number is not the rule’s result.
solution: (b) Multiply each net R by $100 and add: 20,000 → 20,195 → 20,090 → 20,145 → 20,040 → 20,235 → 20,265 → 20,030 → 19,925 → 20,010 → 20,205 → 20,200 → 20,220 → 20,115 → 20,250 → 20,260 → 20,215 → 20,410 → 20,305 → 20,410 → 20,605. Account return = 605 ÷ 20,000 = 3.025%. The running peak of $20,265 (trade 6) is followed by the lowest later value, $19,925 (trade 8): drawdown = $340, and 340 ÷ 20,265 ≈ 1.68%. Gain needed = 340 ÷ 19,925 ≈ 1.71%. Equity first reaches $20,265 or more at trade 17 ($20,410). The smaller dip after trade 4 ($20,040 from a $20,195 peak, 0.77%) is not the maximum.

(c) Without trade 7: (6.05 + 2.35) ÷ 19 = 8.40 ÷ 19 ≈ +0.442R. The gap loss happened under the rule, so it belongs in the result; dropping it measures only how much one observation moves a small-sample average. A trade could be removed only if it were shown to be a data error, with the correction documented.

practice.title: Drawdown when the losses come first
practice.question: Reorder the twenty net results with the eight losses first, in ledger order (−1.05, −1.05, −2.35, −1.05, −0.05, −1.05, −0.45, −1.05), followed by the twelve wins in ledger order. Starting at $20,000 with $100 per R, find the trough, the maximum drawdown in dollars and percent, the percentage gain needed to recover, and the trade at which the account first returns to $20,000.
solution: The eight losses total −8.10R, or −$810, so equity bottoms at $20,000 − $810 = $19,190 after trade 8. The peak before it is the $20,000 start, so maximum drawdown = $810 ÷ $20,000 = 4.05%.

Recovery needs $810 ÷ $19,190 ≈ 4.22%. The wins in order add $195, $55, $195, $30, $85, $195, $20, $135, giving running gains of $195, $250, $445, $475, $560, $755, $775, and $910. The account first reaches at least $20,000 after the eighth win, which is trade 16, at $19,190 + $910 = $20,100.
Ending equity is still $20,605 and expectancy still +0.3025R. Only the path, and therefore the drawdown, changed.

practice.title: Break-even win rate with costs
practice.question: An assumed method wins 35% of the time for +3R and otherwise loses 1R, before costs. Average costs are 0.12R per trade. Compute gross and net expectancy, then the break-even win rate before and after costs.
solution: Before costs, the break-even win rate p solves 3p = 1 × (1 − p), so p = 1 ÷ 4 = 25%. After costs, 2.88p = 1.12(1 − p), so p = 1.12 ÷ 4.00 = 28%. Costs raise the win rate the method needs by three percentage points. These are assumed probabilities and payoffs, not estimates.

practice.title: Evaluate a confident claim
practice.question: A reader looks at the twenty-trade record and writes: “Twelve wins in twenty and +0.30R per trade. This rule works.” Using only numbers from this chapter, write a short reply that separates what the record shows from what it cannot show.
solution: A strong reply makes four points. First, the arithmetic is right: 60% net wins and +0.3025R expectancy after the modeled $5 cost. Second, the estimate is fragile: removing one +1.95R trade gives +0.22R, removing the gap loss gives +0.44R, and the rough ±2 standard-error band runs from about −0.28R to +0.89R, which includes zero.

Third, the 95% Wilson interval for the win rate is about 38.7% to 78.1%, which includes the sample-based 46.2% break-even. Both payoff estimates are uncertain too, so this comparison does not constitute an expectancy test. Fourth, the record does not show whether trades were clustered in time or shared a market driver; if they were, independence fails and these intervals are too narrow. These fictional outcomes teach calculations; establishing a real rule’s merit needs independent evaluation, a suitable comparator, and execution evidence.

quiz.question: Maya’s twenty net results contain 12 wins averaging +1.18R and 8 losses averaging −1.01R. A colleague reports expectancy as 1.18 − 1.01 = +0.17R. What is the correction?
options: Divide the difference by the number of trades: (1.18 − 1.01) ÷ 20 ≈ +0.01R per trade.
Use the gross averages instead, because the $5 cost is already built into the $100 R denominator.
Weight each average by its frequency: 0.60 × 1.18 − 0.40 × 1.01 ≈ +0.30R, which matches the direct average of the twenty net results.
quiz.explanation: Expectancy weights the average win and the average loss by how often each occurs. The result matches 6.05R ÷ 20 = +0.3025R.
feedback: Subtracting the two group averages omits their 60%/40% frequencies. Dividing that unweighted difference by 20 does not repair the error; the direct method divides the sum of all outcomes by 20.
The R denominator is the $100 planned price risk only; costs are recorded separately and must be subtracted. Gross figures would overstate expectancy by 0.05R per trade.
Correct: with 60% wins and 40% losses, the weighted result equals the total net R divided by the number of trades.

evidence.limits: The ±2 SE band is a teaching approximation assuming independent, identically distributed trades; with n = 20 and lumpy outcomes it is crude.

evidence.claim: The Wilson score interval for 12 wins in 20 trials is about 38.66%–78.12%
evidence.location: NIST Dataplot AGRESTI COULL, Wilson formula; NIST handbook 7.2.4.1, Wilson/proportion interval expression.
evidence.summary: Independently evaluated the Wilson formula at 12/20 with z = 1.95996398454. Both the current NIST handbook page and Dataplot documentation contain the Wilson score expression; other interval methods are separately described.
evidence.limits: Assumes independent Bernoulli trials with a common probability; it does not describe payoff sizes or expected profit.

evidence.claim: Sharpe ratio time-scaling by the square root of T assumes zero serial correlation
evidence.location: Sharpe (1994), “The Ratio” and “Time Dependence” sections
evidence.summary: Read the ex post definition (average differential return ÷ its standard deviation) and the statement that the T-period ratio equals the one-period ratio × √T when differential returns have zero serial correlation.
evidence.limits: Definitions only; the chapter computes no Sharpe ratio for the fictional ledger, and per-trade mean/SD is explicitly not one.

evidence.claim: A p-value is computed under a null hypothesis and its threshold should be set in advance
evidence.location: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook 7.1.3.1, Critical values and p values
evidence.summary: Read the definition (probability of a test statistic at least as extreme as observed, given the null) and the advice to decide the rejection threshold before seeing results. The 1 − 0.95⁶ ≈ 26% figure is the chapter’s own arithmetic for six independent tests.
evidence.limits: The source does not address trading-rule searches; the six-variant figure assumes independence that overlapping variants do not have.

evidence.claim: Selecting among many tested configurations inflates apparent performance
evidence.location: Bailey, Borwein, López de Prado & Zhu, introduction and “Comparisons to other approaches” (pp. 4–7)
evidence.summary: Read the argument that published backtests rarely declare the number of trials, that calibration can fit noise, and that hold-out ignores the number of trials attempted.
evidence.limits: The paper’s PBO/CSCV estimate is not computed in this chapter.

evidence.claim: A large multiple-testing study of technical rules is summarized in the research section
evidence.location: Author-hosted manuscript (sample ends July 2011): introduction p. 3; sections 4–5, pp. 20–25; Table 5, p. 49 (PDF page 49).
evidence.summary: Inspected the author-hosted sample and selection procedure, chronological persistence, and Table 5’s Sharpe-criterion portfolios. FDR break-even one-way costs are 30–35, 0–5 and 0–5 basis points in the first three periods; later FDR portfolios are negative before costs. The authors raise costs inside the monthly ex ante selection until the selected portfolios’ out-of-sample performance disappears (Table 5, p. 24) and call these break-even transaction costs computed ex ante (pp. 22, 24); they criticize break-evens computed after rules are chosen as ex post (p. 21). Either kind is a backtest threshold, not a measurement of the costs an investor would actually pay.
evidence.limits: Index-level experiment; not a test of the book’s fictional rules or of individual-stock methods generally.

study.sample: Daily DJIA index prices, January 1897–July 2011; author-hosted manuscript; the PDF text carries no version date.
study.rule: 7,846 technical rules; multiple-testing adjustment; ex ante rule portfolios updated monthly and evaluated in subsequent periods.
study.comparator: Zero excess-performance threshold and chronological persistence; Table 5 uses the Sharpe-ratio criterion.
study.costs: Table 5 FDR break-even one-way costs: 30–35, 0–5, 0–5 basis points in the first three periods; short lending costs treated separately.
study.result: Past winners cannot reliably be selected to persist; plausible costs erase remaining early-period out-of-sample gains; later FDR portfolios are negative before costs.

evidence.claim: Confidence describes long-run interval-procedure coverage
evidence.location: NIST 1.3.5.2, Purpose/Interval Estimate for Mean and Definition: Confidence Interval.
evidence.summary: Read the repeated-sample interpretation, s/√N term and t multiplier; compare with the textbook’s explicitly crude ±2 SE illustration.
evidence.limits: The source does not validate dependent, nonstationary trade outcomes or the fictional band as an exact 95% interval.

chapters.title: Designing a complete trading system
chapters.subtitle: A signal is one component of a much larger decision process.
chapters.takeaway: A complete system specifies data, eligibility, ranking, sizing, fills, exits, and accounting so precisely that two people processing the same inputs produce the same ledger.
outcomes: Screen, rank with a deterministic tie-break, and size simultaneous candidates as the smallest of the risk, notional, and cash allowances.
Process fills, partial fills, nonfills, halts, gaps, same-bar ambiguity, and time exits in a declared order.
Keep a ledger in which cash + holdings = equity at every close, with reserved cash and costs, and report net R on each trade’s frozen 1R.
Distinguish definitions, conventions, and arbitrary teaching settings, and explain why any rule change, including a regime filter, is a new version.

sections.title: Start with an economic question
paragraphs: A trading system is an organized set of decisions that can be applied consistently. It need not be automated, but its rules should be clear enough to evaluate. Begin with a proposed mechanism and an observable claim. “Trends may persist over this horizon” is a research hypothesis. “This indicator predicts everything” is not a useful specification. The mechanism does not prove an edge; it tells you what evidence would support or weaken the idea.

Chapter 24 tested a twenty-session breakout signal one trade at a time, as though capital and position slots were unlimited. This chapter builds Atlas-20, a complete fictional research system around the same kind of daily breakout signal, and makes every remaining decision explicit. It freezes version 1.0 of the rule sheet, supplies a small invented market of eight stocks over eight sessions, and processes each decision in order until the ledger reconciles to the cent. All companies, prices, volumes, and calendars are fictional. The percentages are teaching settings, not recommended allocations, and the system has no demonstrated performance. The scenario was built to exercise the rules, including a tie, a partial fill, an unfilled order, a halt, and other exceptions, so it is not a typical week.

Use one test for completeness: two careful readers given the same inputs should produce the same ledger without asking the author anything. Each rule below is labeled as a definition, a modeling convention, a scope choice, or an arbitrary teaching setting. The included scripts/atlas20-sim.cjs processes the supplied scenario under the rule sheet and reproduces its accounting; it is a teaching simulator, not a trading engine. You can also reproduce every number by hand from this chapter’s tables.

sections.title: Write the data and eligibility contract
paragraphs: Atlas-20 uses a point-in-time universe and completed regular-session daily bars. “Point in time” means the system uses the member list, prices, and calendar as they were known at each decision close, not as they are known today. The signal needs the twenty sessions before the decision day, so a stock needs 21 consecutive valid bars before it can be screened. If any of those bars is missing, v1.0 records an incomplete record and evaluates nothing that day. It does not fill the gap with yesterday’s price, because an invented bar could create or hide a breakout.

Each filter is part of the research claim, so each is stated with its data and timing. The liquidity filter averages close × volume over the twenty sessions ending at the decision close. A cutoff chosen from the full sample would quietly use the future. The price band keeps the fixed $2 stop between 2% and 10% of the share price. Without it, the same rule would mean very different risks for a $15 stock and a $150 stock. The earnings exclusion covers sessions t+1 through t+10 because this is the planned ten-session holding window for an entry in t+1 (holding session 1), ending at t+10 (holding session 10), so entries exclude announcements known at the decision close within that window. A rescheduled or unexpected announcement remains possible; the calendar is not insurance. The checks run in a declared order, and the first failure is recorded. That keeps the record of skipped candidates honest. A halt can extend the actual elapsed holding beyond that planned window; the calendar filter cannot exclude every announcement during an overdue holding.

sections.title: Translate a signal into portfolio decisions
paragraphs: An eligible stock signals when its completed close exceeds the highest high of the prior twenty completed sessions. When several qualify at the same close, Atlas-20 ranks them by breakout margin, the percentage by which the close clears that high. Rank the margin rounded to 0.01 percentage point, as stated in the table; ties in that rounded value are broken alphabetically. Two unequal raw margins can therefore receive the same rank value. Do not silently switch to unrounded ranking. This rule is not wise or optimized. Its only virtue is that it is written down. Without a declared order, a backtest quietly selects candidates by file order or by whichever result the researcher noticed first.

At most five slots exist, and a slot is occupied by any open position, including a halted one, and by any order placed at the current close. Each order’s quantity is the smallest of three allowances computed from equity E at the decision close. The risk allowance spends at most 0.5% of E on planned price risk at $2 per share. The notional allowance keeps the position at or below 10% of E at the limit price. The cash allowance uses only cash not already reserved for an order placed earlier at the same close. Following the book’s contract, 1R is the frozen planned price risk: filled shares × $2.00, fixed at the fill. The $5 round-trip cost is shown separately. So an ordinary stop exit for a full 250-share position loses $500 of price and $505 including costs. That cost-inclusive figure is a separate, labeled quantity, not 1R.

The cash test deserves a remark. Five slots at a 10% notional cap can commit only about half of equity, so cash does not bind in this unleveraged, mildly varying scenario. Large mark changes, stale valuations, or a later version can make the cash test important; the entry caps do not bound subsequent market values. It is still computed at every decision, for two reasons. Reservations must prevent the same dollars from funding two orders, and any later version with larger caps or more slots can make cash bind. One of the practice tasks shows such a variant.

sections.title: Exits, gaps, and time are first-class rules
paragraphs: Entries use a day-limit buy order for the next session at 1.01 × the signal close, rounded down to the cent. Investor.gov explains that a buy limit executes only at its limit or lower and is not guaranteed to execute, and that a day order generally cancels at the end of the regular session. Atlas-20 models those facts with deliberately conservative conventions. An open at or below the limit fills at the open. A later trade strictly below the limit fills at the limit. A low exactly equal to the limit shows only that the price was touched, which does not prove that shares were available, so it is not a fill. The filled quantity is capped at 1% of the session’s share volume, and the rest of the order is canceled.

Each fill receives a sell stop $2.00 below and a sell limit target $4.00 above the actual fill price, plus a time exit at the close of the tenth holding session. Investor.gov notes that a stop becomes a market order once its price is reached and can execute well away from that price. Atlas-20 therefore models an ordinary stop at the stop price, an opening gap through the stop at the open, and a bar that contains both levels as a stop. Daily data cannot show which level traded first, and assuming the favorable order would flatter the record. These are assumptions about fills, not reports of actual executions.

A trading halt is a different problem. According to Investor.gov, the most common regulatory halt occurs when news is pending, and securities exchanges, not the SEC, decide whether to impose it; other U.S. markets honor a halt imposed by the security’s primary market. While a held stock has no bar, no exit can be modeled. Atlas-20 marks the stock at its last valid close, flags that mark as stale, keeps the slot occupied, and applies the gap rule to the first new bar. Cash earns nothing, settlement timing is ignored, and short sales, leverage, and derivatives are outside the scope of v1.0.

The 1% volume cap is a retrospective daily-bar fill model: the total session volume is unknown at the opening trade. It cannot be used as an instruction for how many shares to execute at that open. A live participation algorithm would need intraday volume and quote data, which this scenario does not provide. There are no splits, dividends, membership changes or calendar revisions during these eight sessions; a deployment specification would need separate policies for them. The supplied rolling-high, liquidity and completeness fields are sufficient statistics for this exercise, not a full historical feed.

If a halt spans holding-session-10 close, record an overdue time exit and retain the slot and stale mark. At the first subsequent tradable opening, opening stop/target gap rules have priority; otherwise exit at that open for the overdue deadline, before considering that bar’s intraday range. For entry E1 and a halt at E10–E12, a reopening at E13 executes this overdue rule. E10 remains the scheduled date; E13 is the later modeled execution date.

Hazel’s tenth holding session is session 2; Fir’s would be session 7. The screen log is supplied data. It lists every stock that was not held and whose close exceeded its prior-20 high at a decision close, along with the pre-computed liquidity, the calendar, and the completeness facts. Every unlisted non-held stock and decision-close pair did not signal. Held stocks are excluded before screening; their omission says nothing about whether their close exceeded a rolling high. The two price grids supply each bar the rules need. A dash means the bar is not needed because the stock was neither held nor being bought. “No bar” means the record does not exist.
Before reading on, apply the rule sheet to decision close 0 yourself. List the six signals, decide which are eligible, rank them, and size whatever fits in the free slots.

sections.title: Decision close 0: four eligible candidates, three slots
paragraphs: Six stocks signal. Elm is excluded because its scheduled earnings fall in session 6, inside the window from session 1 to session 10. Ginkgo is excluded because its mean dollar volume of $1.6 million is below the $2.0 million threshold. Both would have looked attractive on a chart, and both stay in the opportunity record as ineligible. The remaining four rank as Alder at 3.10%, Birch at 2.50%, and then Cedar and Dogwood tied at exactly 2.00%. Cedar wins the tie alphabetically. Hazel and Fir occupy two of the five slots, so only three are free, and Dogwood is recorded as “eligible, no free slot.”

At E = $100,000.00, the risk allowance is floor(500 ÷ 2) = 250 shares for every candidate. Alder’s limit is $32.27, so its notional allowance is floor(10,000 ÷ 32.27) = 309, and risk binds at 250 shares. Birch’s limit is $72.46, so notional binds at 138 shares, which is $9,999.48 at the limit. Cedar’s notional allowance is 242 shares at $41.20. The cash allowances, computed in rank order after earlier reservations, are far larger. The three reservations total $28,044.88 and leave $53,285.12 available. The same price-risk rule produces a full-risk Alder order and two smaller orders because the notional cap binds for the higher-priced stocks.

sections.title: Sessions 1–3: fills, a nonfill, a time exit, and a halt
paragraphs: Session 1 begins with the held positions. Hazel’s range stays between its $45 stop and $51 target. Fir’s low of $34.60 stays above its $34.00 stop. Next come the entries. Alder opens at $32.10, below its $32.27 limit, so all 250 shares fill at the open. Its stop is $30.10, its target is $36.10, and 1R is $500. Birch opens at $72.20, within its limit, but only 11,800 shares trade, so the 1% cap allows 118 of the 138 shares ordered. The remainder cancels, and Birch’s 1R is 118 × $2 = $236, not the $276 planned at the order. Cedar opens at $41.60, above its $41.20 limit, and its low is exactly $41.20. That is a touch, so there is no fill, and the $9,972.90 reservation is released. Cash falls from $81,330.00 by $8,027.50 and $8,522.10 to $64,780.40, and equity at the close is $100,028.30.

Cedar’s unused slot does not go back to Dogwood, because candidates are offered only at their own signal close. Dogwood earns a new chance by signaling again at decision close 1: its $62.40 close exceeds the new prior-20 high of $61.50. The 158-share order reflects the notional allowance, floor(10,002.83 ÷ 63.02). In session 2, Dogwood opens at $62.80, below its limit, and fills there. Hazel reaches holding session 10 without touching either level and exits at the $49.30 close for +$455 net, or +1.14R on its $400 denominator. At decision close 2, Cedar signals again at $42.30, above the $41.95 high it set in session 1, and receives a 234-share order at $42.72.

In session 3, Fir has no bar: trading is halted. Fir is marked at its session-2 close of $35.10 and flagged stale, and the missing bar fires an operational review trigger. Cedar opens at $43.00, above its limit, then trades down to $42.50, so the model fills it at $42.72. Because the fill happened intraday, the entry bar cannot credit a target, and the stop is not reached. At the close, five slots are in use: Fir, Alder, Birch, Dogwood, and Cedar. Hazel then signals at $51.80 and passes every filter, but the halted Fir still holds a slot, so Hazel gets no order. Equity is $100,502.82, and holdings are 45.6% of it, the highest exposure so far.
Pause here. The worksheet below starts from this session-3 state and asks you to process sessions 4 and 5 before you open the complete ledger.

sections.title: Sessions 4–7 and the complete ledger
paragraphs: Fir resumes trading in session 4 with an open of $33.10, below its $34.00 stop, so the exit occurs at the open. The loss is −$725 of price and −$730 net, or −1.46R. That is well beyond the ordinary $505 cost-inclusive modeled loss, because the gap skipped the stop price. In session 5, Birch trades from $70.00 to $76.60, a bar that contains both its $70.20 stop and its $76.20 target. The conservative priority records a stop: −$241 net, or −1.02R. A reader who assumed the target came first would report +$467, or +1.98R. A single unverifiable assumption about the order of trades moves this result by three R. At decision close 5, Ginkgo’s close is above its prior-20 high, but its session-3 bar is missing from the record, so nothing is evaluated.

Alder trades above its $36.10 target in session 6 and exits there for +$995 net, or +1.99R. At that close, Elm signals again. Its earnings date of session 6 is now in the past, and its next scheduled report falls outside the window. It receives a 168-share order, which fills at the $59.10 open of session 7. The scenario ends with Dogwood, Cedar, and Elm open and marked at the session-7 close.

Every row of the ledger satisfies cash + holdings = equity. Equity rises from $100,000.00 to $100,739.22, a change of $739.22. Measured from the session-0 marks, the closed trades contribute +$137.50 for Hazel, −$677.50 for Fir, −$241.00 for Birch, and +$995.00 for Alder, a total of $214.00. The three open positions contribute $532.72 of unrealized price gain less $7.50 of entry costs, or $525.22. The total, $214.00 + $525.22, equals the $739.22 change. Nine fills cost $22.50 inside the scenario.

sections.title: What the ledger can and cannot tell you
paragraphs: The +0.74% change over seven sessions is evidence of nothing about Atlas-20’s merit. It comes from four closed trades and three open ones, invented to exercise the rules. What the ledger does show is structural. Exposure peaked at 45.6% in this supplied path. Entry caps constrain orders at their limits; subsequent mark changes can move holdings above those percentages. Slots, not cash, rationed the opportunities: Dogwood at decision close 0 and Hazel at decision close 3 were eligible and turned away. The conventions also matter, though not in one direction. Stop-first turned Birch’s ambiguous bar into −$241 instead of +$467. The participation cap shrank that same losing trade from 138 to 118 shares, which reduced its loss by $40. The touch rule kept Cedar out at $41.20, which changed which candidates later received slots; the supplied bars cannot price that alternative path. Conservative here means not assuming an unproven favorable fill, not always lowering the result.

The ledger also keeps the decisions that never became trades. Elm and Ginkgo were ineligible, Cedar did not fill, Dogwood and Hazel found no free slot, and Ginkgo’s record was incomplete. Testing, discussed in the earlier evidence chapter, needs exactly this full opportunity set. A researcher who keeps only the trades cannot ask whether the ranking rule, the slot limit, or the earnings window is doing useful work. Answering those questions takes many more opportunities than this scenario provides, held-out data, and realistic costs. The case studies in the last chapter return to such records.

sections.title: A regime filter would be version 1.1
paragraphs: A regime filter restricts trading according to a defined market state. Atlas-20 v1.0 has none. Adding one creates a new version that needs its own data contract. A complete specification might read: “No new entries at a decision close unless the fictional benchmark’s completed close exceeds the simple average of its previous 50 completed closes. Existing positions are unaffected. If the benchmark bar is missing, no new entries.” That sentence names the series, the lookback, the timestamp, what the filter blocks, and its missing-data rule. It is still a hypothesis, not an improvement. A filter can skip losing periods and also miss rebounds. If its definition is repeatedly altered to fit the same history, the search grows while the final system appears more careful.

The separate fictional figure contrasts two predetermined exposure schedules over an invented price path. The switching path holds 101 in cash for steps 4–7 and reenters at an index of 92, so its later values equal 101 × index ÷ 92. The figure shows the consequences of exposure timing, not evidence that any filter can identify those dates. In a real test, every switch must follow information available at the time, and cash returns and costs must be included. Measuring only the invested periods would hide the opportunity cost of sitting in cash.

sections.title: Specify when to pause and how to improve
paragraphs: A monitoring plan compares observed behavior with the specification: signal counts, data completeness, exposure, costs, and differences between modeled and actual fills. Atlas-20 separates operational triggers from performance triggers. Fir’s missing bar in session 3 fired an operational trigger. The right response is to confirm the halt and the data feed, not to change a parameter. The scenario’s largest decline from an equity peak, from $100,502.82 to $100,188.02, is about 0.31%, far from the 8% performance trigger. Even a breached trigger only starts a review; a losing week is not proof that the hypothesis has failed.

Any change to the rule sheet, whether a new ranking, a different cap, or a regime filter, becomes a new version with its own record. Bailey and coauthors explain why this matters. The chance of a false discovery rises with the number of configurations tried on the same data, and published backtests rarely report how many trials were run. Keep every version and the reason for it, evaluate on data not used to choose the change, and compare with simpler alternatives. A complete system is valuable because it exposes every decision to scrutiny. It becomes credible only through honest evidence, feasible execution, and a risk policy suited to its uncertainty.

example.title: Two limits disagree
example.text: At decision close 0, equity is $100,000.00 and the risk allowance is 250 shares for every candidate. Alder’s $32.27 limit allows 309 shares under the 10% notional cap, so risk binds at 250 shares: $8,067.50 of notional and a 1R of $500. Birch’s $72.46 limit allows only 138 shares, so notional binds. Its planned risk is $276, but after the partial fill of 118 shares its frozen 1R is $236. The qualifying signal does not override the tighter limit, and the denominator follows the shares actually filled.

chapters.exercise: Start from the session-3 close. Cash is $54,714.02; the holdings are Fir 250 shares (halted, last close $35.10, stop $34.00), Alder 250 (stop $30.10, target $36.10), Birch 118 (stop $70.20, target $76.20), Dogwood 158 (stop $60.80, target $66.80), and Cedar 234 (stop $40.72, target $46.72); no orders are working. Using the rule sheet, the price grids, and the screen log, process session 4, decision close 4, session 5, and decision close 5. For each, record every exit price and reason, cash after the fills, each close mark, equity, free slots, and any order. Then give the net P&L and net R of the Fir and Birch trades.
solution: Session 4, held positions. Fir’s first bar since the halt opens at $33.10, at or below its $34.00 stop, so step 1 exits at the open. Alder: notional floor(40,000 ÷ 32.27) = 1,239 and cash 2,520, so risk binds at 1,000 shares, with a reservation of 1,000 × 32.27 + 2.50 = $32,272.50. Cedar: $9,057.08 remains, so the cash allowance is floor((9,057.08 − 2.50) ÷ 41.20) = 219 shares, below the risk (1,000) and notional (970) allowances. Cash binds at 219 shares, with a reservation of $9,025.30, leaving $31.78. Without reservations, the account would appear to fund three full orders worth more than its cash. practice.title: Diagnose a substituted order
practice.question: A colleague’s ledger shows Dogwood bought during session 1 at its decision-close-0 limit of $61.81. The colleague reasons that Cedar failed to fill, so its slot should pass to the next-ranked candidate. The session-1 open of $61.40 then fills Dogwood below the limit. Identify every rule this record breaks, and give the v1.0 treatment of Dogwood.
solution: First, v1.0 places orders only at a decision close, using information through that close. Cedar’s nonfill became known only during session 1. Second, rejected candidates are not re-offered. Third, Cedar’s reservation and slot are released only when its order expires, and a new slot can be used only at the next decision close. The substitution is a new rule, invented after seeing the outcome, and it would flatter the record by buying $1.40 per share cheaper than v1.0 does.

Under v1.0, Dogwood is recorded as eligible with no free slot at decision close 0. It signals again at decision close 1 and receives 158 shares at a $63.02 limit, filled at the $62.80 open of session 2. Testing a substitution rule properly would mean writing it into a new version and applying it to every opportunity, including the cases where it would buy a loser.

chapters.title: Optional: Dow, Wyckoff, and Elliott, read critically
chapters.subtitle: Apply one core rule from each framework to a fictional chart, and keep description, causal story, and evidence apart.
chapters.takeaway: Each classical framework can be made precise enough to test one claim at a time; its labels, and its advocates’ confidence, do not by themselves establish a trading edge.
outcomes: Classify a two-average Dow-style move as unconfirmed or confirmed by comparing each average’s close with its own reference high, at the close where the classification becomes known.
Apply a frozen spring rule, with a stated breach size and reentry window, to a fictional trading range, and classify the alternative breakdown branch under the same rule.
Check a proposed Elliott impulse count against the three standard rules, and show that more than one count can pass them.
Separate each framework’s descriptive convention, causal story, and empirical claim, and name the evidence each layer would need.

sections.title: What this optional chapter covers
paragraphs: Dow theory, Wyckoff analysis, and Elliott wave analysis are older than most of the indicators in this book, and they still shape market commentary. You will meet sentences such as “the averages have not confirmed,” “that dip looked like a spring,” or “we are in wave three.” This chapter teaches enough of each framework to read those sentences precisely and to test one of their claims. It is an optional branch. Nothing later in the core path depends on it, and it is not a practitioner’s manual.

The scope is deliberately narrow. From Dow theory we take one idea: confirmation between two averages, each judged against its own reference high. The full classification of primary, secondary, and minor movements is left out. From Wyckoff we take the trading range and the spring. Point-and-figure “cause” counts, the full phase schematics, and the distribution events are left out. From Elliott we take the five-wave impulse, its three standard rules, and the idea of alternate counts. Corrective-pattern families, diagonals, and Fibonacci ratio guidelines are left out. Each framework gets its own worked example and its own figure. All of the charts are invented for teaching.

One distinction organizes everything that follows. A framework offers a descriptive convention: what is labeled, from which data, at what time. It usually adds a causal story: why the labeled pattern supposedly happens. Many presentations then make an empirical claim, about later returns or reliability. The three layers need different evidence. A description can be checked by reproducing it. A causal story needs evidence about participants and mechanisms. An empirical claim needs a defined test across many cases. The definitions in this chapter come from CMT Association, Wyckoff Analytics, and Elliott Wave International. These are proponent organizations: they are the right sources for what the frameworks say, but they are not independent evidence that following them earns money.

sections.title: Dow theory: each average against its own reference high
paragraphs: Dow theory grew out of Charles Dow’s editorials and the work of later interpreters. In the CMT Association’s summary, the two averages must confirm each other: a primary uptrend is signaled when both rise above their respective highs of previous upward secondary reactions. Only closing prices count. Confirmation does not have to arrive on the same day or even in the same month, and a nonconfirmation, where one average exceeds its prior extreme while the other does not, is treated as a warning to stay alert, not as a signal in its own right. Historically the averages were industrial and railroad indexes, chosen because they represented related parts of economic activity.

The figure follows two fictional averages, A and B, both indexed to 100 at step 0. At step 3, A closes at 110 and B at 106. Both then decline to step 5, A to 103 and B to 100. For this exercise, treat the rise to step 3 as the previous upward secondary reaction; its step-3 closes are given as the reference highs. Deciding whether a move qualifies as a secondary reaction, and which primary trend it interrupts, needs further rules, which this chapter does not teach. Freeze the teaching rule before reading on: a close strictly above the reference counts, and equality does not; confirmation is recorded at the first completed close at which both averages are above their own references at the same time.

Now walk forward one close at a time. At step 7, A closes at 109 and B at 103; neither has crossed. At step 8, A closes at 112, above 110, while B closes at 104, below 106. That close establishes a nonconfirmation, and nothing more. Through steps 9 and 10, A stays above its reference while B reaches only 103 and 105. At step 11, B closes at 107 while A closes at 113. Both are now above their own references, so confirmation is recorded at the step-11 close, three observations after A’s first crossing, with A at 113, one point above its step-8 close.

Two tempting shortcuts give the wrong answer. At step 8, A is up 12% from the start and B is up 4%, so both are up, but neither gain decides confirmation; only the reference high does. If B’s reference had been 103 instead of 106, the same 104 close would already be above it. And an intraday high above 106 would not count, because the convention uses closes. The test also leaves several decisions open: which averages to use, whether the second crossing may come weeks later, as the source allows, and what action, if any, follows. The empirical claim, that confirmed moves are followed by better outcomes, can only be judged by applying one frozen version of the rule across many episodes, nonconfirmations included.

sections.title: Wyckoff: a range, a spring candidate, and a breakdown branch
paragraphs: Wyckoff analysis organizes price and volume into trading ranges and a repeating cycle of accumulation, markup, distribution, and markdown. Wyckoff Analytics presents three laws: supply and demand, cause and effect, and effort versus result. It describes a spring as a move that takes price below the low of the trading range and then reverses to close within it, and it notes that springs are not required: some accumulation ranges do not have one. The “Composite Man” is a teaching device: the analyst studies the market as if one operator were behind its movements. It helps generate questions about who might be buying or selling. It is not an observation of an actual person.

Here is the fictional range. Over sessions 1 to 16, the reaction lows are $30.00, $30.20, and $30.40 (sessions 4, 9, and 14), and the reaction highs are $34.00, $33.80, and $33.60 (sessions 2, 7, and 12). The first table below lists them beside the closes that the figure plots; a close line alone cannot show them. The figure shades a support zone from $30.00 to $30.40 and a resistance zone from $33.60 to $34.00. A zone is a good way to show where reactions occurred, but a rule needs a single number, so after session 16 support is frozen at the lowest low, $30.00. The spring rule is frozen at the same time. A breach is a completed session whose low is at least 1% below support, that is, $29.70 or lower. A breach becomes a spring candidate at the first completed close strictly above $30.00, counting from the breach session’s own close through the three sessions after it. It becomes a breakdown if none of those four closes is above $30.00. While that window is open, further lows at or below $29.70 belong to the same breach event and do not open a new window; a new event can begin only after the current one is classified. A low between $29.70 and $30.00 is an undercut smaller than this rule’s breach threshold and is not classified. The 1% and three-session settings are this chapter’s own research choices, not canonical Wyckoff values.

Session 17 opens at $30.50, trades as high as $30.60 and as low as $29.50, and closes at $29.80. The breach is (30.00 − 29.50) ÷ 30.00 = 1.67%, so it qualifies. The close of $29.80 is still below support, which means the price has not yet reversed to close inside the range. Our rule therefore has not classified a recovery. At this cutoff the only correct record is “breach; window open.” Calling it a spring, or a breakdown, would be using bars that do not yet exist.

Two continuations share that session-17 record. In the spring branch, session 18 trades between $29.70 and $30.80 and closes at $30.60; its $29.70 low belongs to the open session-17 event rather than starting a new one. That is a close above $30.00 in the first session of the window, so a spring candidate is recorded at the session-18 close; the later closes of $31.00 and $31.40 do not change the classification. In the breakdown branch, sessions 18 to 20 close at $29.40, $29.10, and $28.60. None is above $30.00, so the breakdown is recorded only at the session-20 close, when the window ends. Before that close it was undecided, not “probably a breakdown.”

Notice what the rule has and has not established. The spring branch is a rule event. It says nothing about accumulation by hidden buyers. Wyckoff Analytics interprets a low-volume spring as a sign of readiness to rise; adding a volume condition, such as breach-session volume below its 20-session average, would need its own threshold and would change which breaches count. The causal story remains a hypothesis. The empirical claim requires counting every breach in a defined universe, with both branches kept in the record.

sections.title: Elliott wave: an impulse must pass three rules
paragraphs: Elliott wave analysis classifies swings into nested structures. Elliott Wave International describes an impulse as five subwaves moving in the direction of the next larger trend, and a correction as three subwaves. These patterns combine into larger patterns of the same form, at larger “degrees.” For a standard impulse, EWI states three rules: wave 2 never retraces more than 100% of wave 1; wave 3 is never the shortest of waves 1, 3, and 5; and wave 4 never ends in the price territory of wave 1. EWI distinguishes these rules, which it says govern every impulse, from guidelines such as alternation, extension, and truncation, which describe typical but not inevitable features. Diagonals are a separate pattern family with their own rules, which this chapter does not review. Switching to a diagonal to rescue a count that has broken a rule is a change of classification, and it should be recorded as one.

The schematic in the figure has swing endpoints at $40 (the start, step 0), $44, $42, $50, $47, and $53, followed by $49, $51, and $46. Check the labeled count one rule at a time. Rule 1: wave 2 ends at $42, above the $40 start; it retraces $2 of a $4 advance, or 50%. Rule 2: waves 1, 3, and 5 measure $4, $8, and $6, so wave 3 is the longest, not the shortest. Rule 3: wave 4 ends at $47, above wave 1’s $44 high. The count passes all three rules, and the final $53 → $49 → $51 → $46 sequence is labeled as an A–B–C correction.

Two cautions apply even to this tidy picture. First, the two EWI pages word rule 3 slightly differently: one says wave 4 does not “end in” wave-1 territory, the other that it does not “enter” or overlap it. EWI’s Impulse entry states that the no-overlap form holds for all non-leveraged cash markets, which include the stocks in this book, so this exercise uses it: no point of wave 4 may enter wave-1 territory. The endpoint is its lowest point in this schematic. A real intraday overlap would invalidate this standard-impulse classification even if the close later recovered; the endpoint-only paraphrase is insufficient. Second, the intermediate points are straight-line fillers, not lower-degree waves. A full analysis would also require the impulse to subdivide 5-3-5-3-5, with waves 1, 3, and 5 themselves motive waves, and the schematic does not attempt that.

sections.title: Alternate counts and the timing of a label
paragraphs: EWI states that two or more valid wave interpretations usually exist at any time, and that analysts rank them as “preferred” and “alternate” according to how well each fits the guidelines. The same nine swing points show why. Count B treats the rise from $42 to $53 as one extended wave 3, with $50 and $47 as internal swings. It then labels $49 as wave 4 and $51 as wave 5. Its lengths are $4, $11, and $2, so wave 3 is not the shortest, and wave 4 ends at $49, above $44. Count B passes these three top-level comparisons; subdivisions are not supplied, so this is a candidate count, not a validated impulse. Its fifth wave ends below the end of wave 3, a “truncation,” which EWI treats as a guideline-level feature rather than a rule violation. Count C starts at $42 and labels $50, $47, $53, $49, and $51 as waves 1 through 5. Its wave 4 ends at $49, inside wave 1’s territory below $50, so it fails rule 3.

The top-level checks remove count C, but they cannot choose between candidates A and B. Passing necessary checks is not sufficient to validate either complete wave structure. Those two counts imply different provisional claims at the same moment. At step 12, with price at $49 and no later bar, count A treats the decline from $53 as a possible wave A of a correction and expects a wave-B rally followed by a wave-C decline. Count B treats it as a possible wave 4 and expects a fifth advance. Both expect the next swing to be up, so the next bar cannot separate them, and neither can yet know that $49 is a completed low. Ranking them as preferred and alternate is a judgment about guidelines, and it is exactly the judgment a test must capture. Labels also arrive late. At step 10 no reader could know that $53 was the end of an impulse rather than part of a longer advance. An endpoint label remains provisional until a declared reversal criterion recognizes it; hindsight endpoints cannot be treated as known in real time.

Good practice is to freeze the preferred count, the alternate, and the price that would invalidate each, at every cutoff. At step 12, count B would be invalidated by any trade at or below $44, where wave 4 would enter wave-1 territory. The three impulse rules give count A no invalidation level, because a correction is not an impulse, and this chapter does not teach the corrective-pattern rules that would supply one; the analyst must declare it. If an analyst re-labels after each surprise and keeps only the final count, the method will look continuously right, because the record contains only the interpretation that survived. Three outcomes can then be measured separately: whether the counts obeyed the rules, whether the frozen forecasts were directionally right over a stated horizon, and whether any action based on them earned money after costs. They are different questions.

sections.title: From vocabulary to an honest test
paragraphs: An empirical claim can be tested only one precise proposition at a time, and the proposition has to be fixed before the outcomes are known. The spring rule above is a ready-made example. Apply it to every breach in a defined universe and period, keep both branches, and declare an action in advance: perhaps a next-open entry after the reentry close, a stop below the breach low, a time exit, and modeled costs, the same structure as the breakout plan in Chapter 9 and the casebook in the next chapter. Then compare the outcomes with a stated alternative, such as breaches that did not reenter or all sessions in the same stocks. A favorable result on that one specification would support that one specification, not Wyckoff analysis as a whole.

Where discretion is essential, as in choosing between Elliott counts, test the discretion itself. Ask two readers to label the same charts with the future bars hidden, timestamp their preferred and alternate counts, and keep their disagreements. Measure agreement first, then forecast accuracy, then net results. Lo, Mamaysky, and Wang took another route: they replaced visual judgment with an algorithm that detects chart patterns, then compared returns after detected patterns with ordinary returns in U.S. stocks. Their findings concern their own pattern definitions. They are not tests of Dow confirmation, springs, or wave counts.

This book has not reviewed an independent study that establishes the predictive value of these three frameworks as defined here. That is a statement about the evidence considered, not a proof that they have none. The research appendix summarizes the studies that were examined. Historical influence earns a framework a place in study. Reproducible evidence determines how much confidence any particular claim deserves.

example.title: Disagreement is data
example.text: At the session-17 close of the Wyckoff example, one fictional reader writes “spring developing” and another writes “breakdown under way.” Under the frozen rule, both are premature: the only valid record is a 1.67% breach with the window open. Each reader should still save their label, reasons, invalidation level, and any proposed action before session 18 appears. The later close can then test those frozen interpretations. It cannot tell you what either reader knew at the time.

chapters.exercise: Using the Wyckoff table, state the record for each branch at the session-17, 18, 19, and 20 closes under the frozen spring rule. Then reclassify the spring branch under an alternative, stricter teaching rule requiring the breach session itself to close back inside the range, and explain why the two classifications differ.
solution: Session-17 close: breach size = (30.00 − 29.50) ÷ 30.00 = 0.0167, or 1.67%, which is at least 1% (equivalently, 29.50 ≤ 29.70). A breach is recorded. The breach session’s own close of 29.80 is not above 30.00, so the window stays open through sessions 18–20 and both branches are undecided. They are identical up to this point.

Spring branch: the session-18 close of 30.60 is above 30.00 and inside the window, so a spring candidate is recorded at that close. The session-19 and session-20 closes (31.00, 31.40) do not change the record. Breakdown branch: closes of 29.40, 29.10, and 28.60 are all at or below 30.00. The record stays undecided through session 19 and becomes a breakdown at the session-20 close, when the window ends.

Alternative same-session rule: session 17 closes at 29.80, below support, so neither branch has a spring under that definition. The spring branch’s session-18 recovery would have to be recorded under some other label, such as “breach followed by a later recovery.” Every same-session spring would also be a spring under the frozen rule, so the alternative is strictly stricter; the two definitions still classify these bars differently, so the definition must be frozen before outcomes are counted. Neither version establishes accumulation or predicts the next move.

practice.title: Two versions of confirmation
practice.question: Fictional averages C and D have reference highs of 220 and 85. Their closes are: t0 C 218.0, D 85.0; t1 C 221.0, D 84.2; t2 C 219.5, D 85.4; t3 C 222.4, D 85.3. (a) Under this chapter’s simultaneous-close rule, when is confirmation recorded? (b) Under an alternative rule that records confirmation once each average has closed above its own reference at least once since the reference highs were set, when is it recorded? (c) What does t0 teach?
solution: (a) t1: C 221.0 > 220 but D 84.2 is not above 85, so this is a nonconfirmation. t2: D 85.4 > 85, but C 219.5 has fallen back below 220, so the two are not above at the same close. t3: C 222.4 > 220 and D 85.3 > 85, so confirmation is recorded at t3.
(b) C first closes above at t1 and D first closes above at t2. Once both have crossed, the alternative rule records confirmation at t2, one observation earlier than the simultaneous rule.

(c) At t0, D’s 85.0 equals its reference. Under a strictly-above rule, equality does not count. The two rule versions are both defensible readings of a source that allows lag, which is why the version must be frozen before outcomes are compared.

practice.title: Check a new count before forecasting
practice.question: A reader labels fictional swings $20 (start), $26, $21.50, $30, $25.50, and $31 as waves 0–5 of a standard impulse, then forecasts a decline. Check all three rules, show your arithmetic, and state what the reader must record if they want to keep a bullish or bearish interpretation.
solution: Wave lengths: wave 1 = 26 − 20 = $6; wave 3 = 30 − 21.50 = $8.50; wave 5 = 31 − 25.50 = $5.50. Rule 1: wave 2 ends at 21.50 ≥ 20, a 4.50 ÷ 6 = 75% retracement, so it passes. Rule 2: wave 3 ($8.50) is the longest, so it passes. Rule 3: wave 4 ends at 25.50, below wave 1’s $26 high, so it ends inside wave-1 territory and fails.

The labels are not a valid standard impulse, so the forecast cannot rest on “wave 5 is complete.” The reader can (1) state that no valid impulse count exists here, (2) propose a different structure, such as a diagonal, whose separate rules this chapter does not teach, or (3) change the degree or starting point. Whichever they choose, they should timestamp the new label, record that the original count failed rule 3, and state the new invalidation level, taken from the rules of whichever structure they choose, before the next swing appears. This chapter supplies those rules only for the standard impulse. The overlap is a classification fact. It is not, on its own, evidence about the next direction.

practice.title: Sort framework statements into layers
practice.question: Classify each statement as a descriptive convention, a causal story, or an empirical claim, and name the evidence that would check it. (a) “Both averages closed above their own reference highs at step 11.” (b) “The averages must confirm because industry and transport move together in a genuine expansion.” (c) “Springs in large U.S. stocks are followed by higher 20-session returns than breaches that do not reenter.” (d) “At step 12, count B labels $49 as the end of wave 4.”
solution: (a) Descriptive convention. Check it by reproducing the closes against the frozen simultaneous-close rule; two readers should agree.
(b) Causal story. It needs evidence about economic linkages and participants, not just chart agreement; a reproducible confirmation record cannot establish why it happens.

(c) Empirical claim. It needs one frozen spring rule applied to every breach in a defined universe and period, a stated comparator, a fixed horizon and costs if trades are implied, with both branches kept.

(d) A descriptive label, but a provisional one. It can be checked against the three impulse rules, yet passing them does not validate the count, $49 is not yet a recognized low at step 12, and the label is not by itself a forecast. Its predictive value would be an empirical claim needing frozen, timestamped counts across many charts.

quiz.question: Average A closes at 112 and average B at 104; both started at 100. Their reference highs are 110 and 106. Under this chapter’s closing-price rule, what should be recorded at this close?
options: Unconfirmed: A is above its own reference high, but B’s close is not above 106.
Confirmed: both averages are above their common starting value of 100.
Confirmed, provided B traded as high as 106.50 during the session.
quiz.explanation: Each average is compared with its own reference high, using completed closes. B has not closed above 106, so the record at this close is a nonconfirmation. A later close can change it.
feedback: Correct: 112 > 110, but 104 is not above 106. Record a nonconfirmation at this close, and keep watching for a later close.
This uses the wrong comparator. Confirmation compares each average with its own prior reference high, not with the starting value; percentage gains from 100 do not decide it.
This uses the wrong price field. The convention described here counts closing prices only, so an intraday high above 106 does not confirm.

evidence.claim: Dow confirmation compares each average’s close with its own prior reference extreme, and confirmation may lag.
evidence.location: CMT Association, Technically Speaking, October 2011, “Dow Theory”: principles 5 and 6 and the elaboration on confirmation timing and non-confirmations.
evidence.summary: Re-read on 2026-10-01: both averages must rise above their respective highs of previous upward secondary reactions; only closing prices are considered; confirmation need not occur on the same day or month; non-confirmations function only as warnings. The A/B values and the simultaneous-close rule are this chapter’s own.
evidence.limits: Proponent description. The two-high exercise does not implement the full secondary-reaction classification or establish that confirmation predicts returns.

evidence.claim: A Wyckoff spring is a move below the trading-range low followed by a reversal back inside; springs are not required elements.
evidence.location: Author-hosted tutorial PDF, Composite Man / laws sections, printed pp. 2–4; Accumulation Events and Phase C, pp. 7–9
evidence.summary: Read the author-hosted PDF because the HTML page blocked retrieval. It describes a breach followed by a reversal/close in the range and optional springs, without specifying a one-session deadline. Same-session and three-session limits are explicitly alternative teaching choices.
evidence.limits: Proponent description. The 1% breach and three-session reentry window are the chapter’s own research settings. Statements about large interests and readiness to rise are interpretations, not tested here.

evidence.claim: A standard Elliott impulse is governed by three rules, distinct from guidelines such as alternation and truncation.
evidence.location: EWI, “Elevate Your Elliott Wave Analysis” (statement of the three rules and the rule/guideline distinction); EWI Waveopedia “Impulse” (wave-4 overlap wording; rules versus guidelines).
evidence.summary: Read the rules as worded: wave 2 never retraces more than 100% of wave 1; wave 3 is never the shortest of waves 1, 3 and 5; wave 4 never ends in wave-1 price territory (the Impulse page says it does not enter or overlap it). Checked that truncation is listed among guidelines.
evidence.limits: Classification rules within the method. Passing them is not evidence of forecast accuracy or net profit. Diagonal rules were not reviewed.

evidence.claim: Elliott practitioners expect more than one valid count to exist at a time.
evidence.location: EWI, Introduction to the Wave Principle: passages on five/three structure, degree, and preferred versus alternate interpretations.
evidence.summary: Read that two or more valid wave interpretations usually exist and are ranked as preferred or alternate by guidelines. The page also describes the principle as an objective means of determining probabilities; that is reported as a proponent claim and not evaluated.
evidence.limits: Proponent source; no independent test of count agreement or forecast accuracy was reviewed for this chapter.

evidence.claim: The Dow, Wyckoff, and Elliott worked numbers are internally consistent.
evidence.location: Dow table and panels; spring table and figure; Elliott rule-check table, schematic, exercise and practice solutions.
evidence.summary: Recomputed with a script: first A crossing at step 8 and first simultaneous crossing at step 11; breach 0.5 ÷ 30 = 1.67% and threshold $29.70; reentry at session 18 and breakdown at session 20; wave lengths 4/8/6, 4/11/2, and 8/6/2 with each rule comparison; practice values (t3 and t2 confirmations; 6/8.5/5.5 lengths, 75% retracement, 25.50 < 26 overlap).
evidence.limits: Arithmetic on invented data only.

evidence.claim: The simultaneous-close confirmation rule and the 1%/three-session spring rule are original teaching specifications.
evidence.location: Dow and Wyckoff sections.
evidence.summary: Stated before each worked chronology so that two readers classify the same bars identically; the alternative readings (lagged confirmation, same-session reentry) are shown rather than hidden.
evidence.limits: Arbitrary thresholds; not canonical versions of either framework and not optimized or tested.

evidence.claim: Independent evidence for the predictive value of these three frameworks, as defined here, has not been established in this book.
evidence.location: Final section, “From vocabulary to an honest test.”
evidence.summary: No independent study testing Dow confirmation, the spring rule, or Elliott counts was reviewed for this revision. Lo, Mamaysky and Wang is cited only as an example of algorithmic pattern definition, with its own pattern set.
evidence.limits: Absence of reviewed evidence is not evidence of no effect. A literature search for framework-specific tests remains open.

chapters.title: Case studies: follow the decision through
chapters.subtitle: Successful trades, failed trades, and the decision to stand aside.
chapters.takeaway: A case is a chain from known data through a frozen decision to a later record. Keep favorable, unfavorable, skipped and unresolved cases together; a selected gallery cannot estimate performance.

sections.title: Read a case in three passes
paragraphs: First read the information cutoff and cover the continuation. State what is observed, what is hypothesized and what action is allowed. Second reveal the next observation and apply the frozen rule, including a skip or an unresolved state when appropriate. Third reconcile the result and ask which conclusion it supports. This procedure turns a case from a memorable story into something another reader can reproduce.

The first seven cases below are fictional, purpose-built to exercise different decisions. The historical additions are separately labeled: sparse SEC-reported GME facts, Apple’s split announcement, and a calendar-selected AAPL/MSFT/SPY gallery with exact archived OHLC. The gallery preserves its complete selection ledger and a separately disclosed ambiguity diagnostic. Each source has a stated data/reuse contract. Hypothetical fills in the fictional records are not historical transactions, and the historical path labels do not estimate strategy performance.

Use the completed P1 plan from Chapter 21 for the shared breakout cases. For ATLS, BRDG, SKIP and AMB, the boundary is $50, S0 closes $50.40, the rounded ceiling is $50.90, the maximum order is 50 shares and the fixed stop/target are $48.60/$54.60. The opening gate, first-hour expiry, partial-fill handling, stop-first convention, ten-session time limit and $2.50-per-side fee all remain P1. ATLS’s calendar/account inputs are the same as BRDG’s. Each case starts in its own $20,000 cash account unless noted; never add these selected outcomes into one claimed portfolio history.

sections.title: Case one: follow-through and an orderly failure share a beginning
paragraphs: At S0 the only price-based signal fact is C50.40 > previously frozen 50.00. In both branches the opening offer is $50.60 and a supplied paper execution confirms 50 shares at that price during P1’s allowed hour. The entry debit is $2,532.50 including its $2.50 charge; 1R freezes at $100. Read the OHLC table one session at a time. Neither branch can borrow the other’s outcome to justify the initial decision.

In ATLS, S2 closes $52 after a low 50.70, S3 closes 52.80, and S4 opens 53.80 and trades to 54.80. Its low 52.80 is above the stop, and its high is strictly beyond the target, so the model exits at 54.60. Exit credit $2,727.50 brings cash to $20,195. Gross $200 less $5 costs gives $195/+1.95R. This supplies a successful implementation under the model, not a frequency of target attainment.

BRDG follows the failure record already completed in the plan, note and journal. S2’s close 49.60 weakens the range-continuation interpretation, while its low 49.40 remains above the operational stop. S3 low 48.40 crosses 48.60; the exact-stop model exits at 48.60, yielding −$100 gross, −$105 net and cash $19,895. Rewriting the exit to S2 close after seeing S3 would evaluate a new rule on its discovery case. Both branches follow the initial protocol; their outcomes differ.

sections.title: Case two: a gap passes the protective price
paragraphs: GAPS is a different price-scale case, with a complete smaller rule GR1. At G0, the supplied close is $79.80 above a previously mapped $79.00 boundary; the calendar has no known earnings through G10. The next-opening gate accepts prices above the $77 fixed stop and at or below $80.60. At the supplied G1 open of $80, a paper report fills 30 shares. Freeze 1R = 30 × ($80 − $77) = $90. Target is $86, time exit G10 close, and the same earlier-holding exit priorities and $5 round-trip fee apply.

The entry session has O80/H81/L79/C80.50, so neither level executes. Before G2, unexpected adverse news arrives. G2 has O70/H72/L68/C71, and the opening-gap priority exits at 70. Price loss is 30 × ($70 − $80) = −$300; net −$305; net R = −305 ÷ 90 = −3.3889. Entry debit $2,402.50 and exit credit $2,097.50 reconcile $19,695 final cash. Scheduled-event eligibility did not exclude the surprise.

Reduce quantity to 15 without changing prices or the flat fees. Planned price-risk 1R becomes $45, notional $1,200 and price loss $150, still −3.3333R gross. Net loss is $155, or −3.4444R: halving quantity reduces dollars, but the fixed fee is now a larger fraction of R. If one instead assumed proportional fees, net R could remain unchanged. Name that cost convention before making the comparison; neither smaller sizing nor a different order makes the $77 stop a price guarantee.

sections.title: Case three: the skip is a completed decision
paragraphs: SKIP has P1’s S0 signal and all eligibility inputs, but the supplied S1 opening offer is $52. It exceeds 50.90, so the gate rejects the candidate. No order, position or fee exists. A later S2 close of $56 is revealed only after the decision. Record “opening ceiling; no trade,” not a zero-R scratch. Without a position there is no trade-specific denominator.

The missed advance is observable, and it can motivate a ceiling-change hypothesis. It cannot by itself price the alternative strategy. Buying at 52 and selling at 56 would require two specific, feasible fill assumptions; the later close is not a promise that an order could have filled there. A complete comparison would also keep the high-opening candidates that later fell. This case is retained in Chapter 23’s journal so the opportunity restriction remains inspectable.

sections.title: Case four: two clocks and a daily ambiguity
paragraphs: MIXD isolates a difference between two clocks without an order. At M0, the latest two completed weekly closes are $48.90 and $50.30, up under Chapter 17’s close-direction description. M0 is the first session of a new week, and its daily close is $49.70: down from $50.30 and below a previously frozen $50 boundary. Chapter 17 would give this down day neither the aligned nor the conflicting label, because those labels apply only to upward daily changes; the two clocks simply describe different intervals. Rule M1 uses completed-week direction only as context and requires a daily close strictly above 50 before any next-opening order. M0 supplies no daily signal, so no trade is authorized. Calling the rising weekly context “confirmation” cannot supply the missing daily trigger.

AMB is a separate P1 filled-position branch. At its decision cutoff, it shares the 50-share 50.60 entry, $100 price-risk 1R, stop 48.60 and target 54.60. Its next held-position bar is O50.80/H54.80/L48.20/C51.00. Both stop and target are reached, and the open lies between them. P1 records a stop-first modeled loss of $105/1.05R. A target-first model would give +$195/+1.95R: a $300 or 3R difference caused entirely by a sequence assumption.

Two ordered routes demonstrate what daily OHLC loses: 50.80→54.80→48.20→51.00 can reach the target first; 50.80→48.20→54.80→51.00 can reach the stop first. They share identical OHLC. The daily bar does not select one. The honest record therefore has both a scored MODEL result under P1 and an unresolved true sequence. If no sequence policy had been declared, the case could not be assigned a unique modeled result either.

sections.title: Case five: a range recovery uses the same decision discipline
paragraphs: RIVR adds a setup beyond breakout continuation. At R0, a supplied earlier range runs from $30 to $34. Its support 30 is frozen before a breach bar O30.50/H30.60/L29.50/C29.80. At that close, the only record is “breach; recovery not yet seen.” As in Chapter 27, a breach is a completed session whose low is at least 1% below support ($29.70 or lower). Rule RR1 opens one recovery window, from the breach session’s own close through the next three sessions; later lows inside that window belong to the same breach event and do not restart it. The first close in the window strictly above 30 and no higher than 34 is the recovery trigger. It is a defined range-recovery study, not proof of hidden accumulation or a complete Wyckoff analysis.

At R1 the stock has O29.90/H30.80/L29.70/C30.60. R1’s own $29.70 low belongs to the open R0 breach event rather than starting a new one, and its completed close meets RR1’s trigger. Freeze an entry rule for R2: accept the next open only in ($29.00, $31.00], buy 50 shares at that supplied opening execution, then use a fixed $29 stop and $35 target, R11 close time exit (ten holding sessions from R2), P1’s stop-first conflict policy and $5 round-trip costs. Account and calendar are clear through R11. Quantity is fixed but price-risk varies with the actual fill; an opening price above $31.00 would instead be a skip.

The accepted R2 bar is O31.00/H32.20/L30.80/C32.00, and a supplied paper report fills 50 at 31.00. Price-risk 1R = 50 × (31−29) = $100; the completed R1 signal did not justify a buy at its earlier 29.90 open. The R3 bar is O32.10/H33.80/L31.80/C33.50. R4 is O34.00/H35.20/L33.70/C34.90, trading strictly above 35 without reaching 29, so the model exits at 35. Gross is $200, net $195/+1.95R, ending cash $20,195. Choosing a $31 ceiling is an arbitrary teaching setting, written at R1, not selected for this ending.

A failed alternative shares R0–R2, then gives R3 O30.70/H31.20/L28.80/C29.20. The modeled 29 stop yields −$100 gross, −$105 net and −1.05R. A missing R1 close would leave recovery eligibility unresolved and create no order. A third branch opens 31.20 at R2, above the 31 ceiling, and is skipped even if it later reaches 35. Keep all such dispositions when designing a study; a recovery label does not guarantee a recovery trade.

sections.title: Compare records without claiming a strategy sample
paragraphs: The completed summary distinguishes a trade’s net P&L from a skip and an unresolved execution fact. Each filled result reports its own frozen price-risk denominator and its separate fee model. The gap uses a different price scale and stop distance; the recovery uses a different trigger. Summing their R as if they were interchangeable observations from one locked rule would obscure the very distinctions the cases teach.

Selection explains what this casebook can support. We deliberately chose follow-through, ordinary loss, gap, skip, conflict and recovery paths. Those cases demonstrate rule application; they were not sampled from a real opportunity set. A count of winners in the gallery would mostly measure the author’s selection. Chapter 24 shows how a frozen research rule and chronological evaluation window address a different question.

The historical additions that follow have distinct evidence contracts. Sparse source facts teach when an execution claim must stop; the calendar-selected archive gallery supplies small OHLC windows with retrospective adjustments and undocumented session details. Apply the same three-pass method: freeze the stated clock, identify missing inputs and distinguish later classifications from the earlier decision. Neither documented market facts nor a systematically recorded gallery turn a hypothetical fill into a historical transaction.
