example.text: GAPS, 30 shares: 1R $90, gross loss $300, costs $5, net −$305/−3.3889R. At 15 shares, 1R $45, gross loss $150, costs still $5, net −$155/−3.4444R. Gross R stays −3.3333; net R worsens slightly because the flat fee is a larger share of planned risk.

practice.title: Audit the ambiguous account
practice.question: Use P1’s conventions on an unfamiliar fictional bar: a $20,000 account, 40 shares filled at $25.00, stop $24.00, target $27.00, $5 round-trip cost and stop-first resolution of an ambiguous bar. (a) The first held bar is O25.20/H27.30/L23.80/C26.10. Give 1R, the stop-first and target-first net results in dollars and R, the ending cash under each, and the size of the difference. (b) Suppose instead the bar is O23.90/H27.30/L23.80/C26.10. What does P1 record, and why is there no sequence ambiguity? (c) Write the review sentence that keeps the modeled result separate from what the bar can show.
solution: (a) 1R = 40 × ($25.00 − $24.00) = $40. The open $25.20 lies between the levels, and the bar reaches both. Stop-first: 40 × (24.00 − 25.00) = −$40 gross, −$45 net, −45 ÷ 40 = −1.125R; ending cash $20,000 − $45 = $19,955. Target-first: 40 × (27.00 − 25.00) = +$80 gross, +$75 net, +1.875R; ending cash $20,075. The difference is $120, or exactly 3R, and it comes entirely from the assumed order of trades inside one bar.

(b) The open $23.90 is already below the $24.00 stop, so P1’s opening-gap priority exits at the open before any later high is considered: 40 × (23.90 − 25.00) = −$44 gross, −$49 net, −49 ÷ 40 = −1.225R. The 1R denominator stays $40. The later $27.30 high cannot have been reached by a position that had already exited.

(c) For (a): “Modeled stop-first result −$45/−1.125R under P1’s declared convention; the bar touched both levels and the true sequence is unresolved from daily OHLC.” Full credit requires the fill-model label, the original $40 denominator, the $5 cost in both branches and no claim about the actual intraday order.

learnerAttempt.title: First pass: four historical cutoffs
paragraphs: Attempt each cutoff before revealing the casebook, outcome headings or complete calendar ledger. These four windows were selected as teaching representatives after inspecting the fixed calendar set; they are not a blind sample or a performance trial. Selection details and all 36 windows remain in the continuation reference.

For each six-row window, compute the mean of the five context closes. Open an observation window only when the cutoff close is strictly above that mean. If it passes, freeze boundaries at 0.99 × cutoff close and 1.01 × cutoff close without rounding. At each of the next five archive bars, first compare the open with both boundaries; if strictly inside, compare the low/high. A sole upper touch is favorable, a sole lower touch adverse, both touches ambiguous; the first resolving observation ends the check. No touch by the fifth bar is unresolved. If the gate fails, keep the skip without a return or R. These are path labels, not trades.

At the cutoff, record eligibility, exact thresholds (if any), information available and what later data would be needed. Do not predict which path will occur. After the reveal, reconcile your original note with the archived continuation without editing the note.

Data are the preserved AAPL/MSFT/SPY educational archive, archive-adjusted USD with undocumented adjustment algorithm and exact session/time-zone. Depositor metadata declares CC0; upstream provenance and point-in-time vintage are limited. These rows are not certified contemporaneous quotes or executable fills. Full files, hashes and provenance are in data/historical/ and the continuation reference.

glossary: Estimated loss under the original sizing and execution assumptions; actual loss can differ.
Choosing the share quantity subject to risk, capital, concentration, and execution constraints.
Position quantity multiplied by price; distinct from a planned loss budget.

In this edition, net trade P&L after costs divided by frozen filled-position price-risk: actual filled shares × (entry fill price − original stop) for a long position. Costs are excluded from this denominator; the maximum order risk budget is a different quantity. State any alternative convention explicitly; an unfilled order has no position-specific R.
Percentage decline from a prior equity peak to a later value.
A specified observation that weakens or rejects the trade hypothesis.
A recorded protocol specifying eligibility, signal, execution, sizing, exits, and contingencies.
An exit governed by elapsed time or a holding-period limit rather than a price target.
A tendency to realize gains more readily than losses.
Selecting or interpreting evidence preferentially in support of an existing belief.
Judging the quality of a decision chiefly from its later result.
Agreement between assigned forecast probabilities and observed frequencies across relevant repeated cases.
The greatest favorable price excursion from entry during a defined holding interval.
The greatest adverse price excursion from entry during a defined holding interval.
All candidates covered by the declared eligibility or study criteria, including retained skips.
A historical simulation of a specified decision rule, portfolio process, and execution model.
Use of information that was unavailable at the simulated decision time.
Distortion from excluding securities or strategies that disappeared from the observed sample.
Selecting historical accidents as if they were relationships that will generalize.
Evaluation on data kept outside the iterative rule-development process.
Average result per outcome under a specified distribution or sample and cost convention.
An interval produced by a procedure with stated long-run coverage under its statistical assumptions.
Mean differential or excess return divided by its standard deviation over a consistent interval.
Probability under a specified null model of a statistic at least as extreme as the observed value by the test definition.
A rule restricting activity according to a defined market-state condition.
Agreement between the specified trends or signals of relevant market averages.
A move below trading-range support followed by return into the range, interpreted as a possible reversal setup.
A different Elliott-wave interpretation that remains compatible with the method’s counting constraints.
Repeated chronological testing: develop and lock a rule on earlier data, evaluate it on the next window, then advance and repeat.
Transaction cost that exactly offsets gross performance in a given sample; specify per-share, per-trade or value-proportional units and a one-way or round-trip convention.
A record of every rule version tried during development, with its result, so the size of the search remains visible.
The share of completed trades with a positive result under a declared convention for costs and break-even trades.
The largest decline from a running equity peak to a later low in a recorded path, usually stated in dollars and percent of the peak.
A chart of the percentage by which equity sits below its running peak at each point; it returns to zero at each new peak.
The estimated sampling variability of a statistic, such as a mean; for a mean of independent observations, the standard deviation divided by the square root of the count.
The win rate at which expectancy is zero for given average win and loss sizes: average loss ÷ (average win + average loss).
Cash set aside for a working order (shares × limit price + modeled cost) so that it cannot fund another order.
A modeling limit on fill size expressed as a fraction of the session’s traded volume.
A valuation at the last valid price when no current price exists, such as during a trading halt; it is flagged rather than treated as a fresh observation.
In Dow theory, a close at which one average exceeds its reference extreme while the other has not; treated as a warning, not a signal.
In Elliott wave analysis, a five-wave motive structure with required subdivisions and counting/non-overlap rules; three endpoint checks alone do not validate a complete count.
A period in which price moves between identifiable support and resistance areas without a sustained trend.

risk.title: Process review: one complete record, from budget to review

tasks.title: Size a cost-inclusive plan
tasks.question: Unfamiliar fictional stock: entry $32/stop $30.50, $90 cost-inclusive budget, $0.12/share round-trip costs, $1,600 notional cap and ample cash. Compute shares, notional, 1R, ordinary net loss and net R if it gaps to $28. Split costs equally between sides. For this arithmetic, model the entry at $32 and the exit at the stated stop or gap price; actual stop execution may differ.
solution: Budget allowance = floor(90/1.62) = 55; notional allowance = floor(1600/32) = 50; use 50. Notional $1,600; entry charge $3; price-risk 1R $75; ordinary net loss $81/−1.08R. Gap price loss $200 plus $6 costs = $206; net R−2.7467.

tasks.title: Complete a decision and a partial fill
tasks.question: A frozen range edge is $40; a completed close is $40.30. Rule: opening offer must be strictly above the $38.70 stop and at or below the $40.70 ceiling; if it passes, submit one day buy limit at $40.70 for at most 50 shares. Keep a confirmed partial fill and cancel the remainder, with no retry. Standing stop $38.70/target $44.70; model stop first if both levels occur in a held-position bar. Costs are $2.50 per executed side. Required calendar and account checks pass. The opening offer is $40.70; a supplied execution report confirms 20 shares at $40.70. A cancellation report confirms the remaining 30 shares canceled before the next bar. Write the entry and review fields if that later held-position bar is O40.80/H44.90/L38.50/C41. Apply the declared exact-stop model; OHLC alone does not prove a real fill or the true stop/target sequence.
solution: The supplied reports establish order 50/fill 20 at $40.70/cancel 30 before the later bar; the opening offer alone would not establish those fills. Entry debit = 20 × $40.70 + $2.50 = $816.50; frozen 1R = 20 × ($40.70−$38.70) = $40. The later held bar opens inside both exit levels and reaches both; modeled stop $38.70 gives gross −$40, net −$45/−1.125R. Exit credit = 20 × $38.70−$2.50 = $771.50. Cash change is −$816.50+$771.50 = −$45. Preserve true sequence as unresolved; compliance under the supplied contract and modeled loss are separate fields.

tasks.title: Review without rewriting
tasks.question: That trade loses; a separate candidate fails the opening ceiling then rallies. The supplied frozen record contains the original signal and execution rules, but no pre-outcome counterargument or probability estimate. Write an appended review that preserves the available record, identifies those missing fields without inventing them, and proposes defensible future research.
solution: Keep the supplied original signal and exit priority unchanged. Mark the pre-outcome counterargument and probability estimate as not recorded; do not write a hindsight objection as though it existed before entry. A missing note is a record-quality limitation, not by itself a violation of an execution rule that never required that field. Record the loss under the declared model and the gate rejection as a nontrade with no R denominator. A ceiling relaxation or close-exit rule is a new version motivated by discovery cases. Freeze it and compare later opportunities, including rebounds and losing gaps. Do not diagnose motive or promise improved returns from journaling.

advanced.title: Evidence review: evaluate a claim, then process a system

tasks.title: Convert a performance claim into checkable arithmetic
tasks.question: A fictional locked study has 10 nonoverlapping trades, each 1R $80: four gross +2R, five −1R, one −2R gap. Flat costs $4/trade. Account starts $10,000 with fixed-dollar sizing. Compute gross/net expectancy, net account return and flat break-even cost. Can it validate the rule?
solution: Gross R = 8−5−2 = 1R; gross $80. Costs $40 = 0.5R, net $40 = 0.5R; gross expectancy 0.10R and net 0.05R. Net account return $40 ÷ $10,000 = 0.4% (gross 0.8%); break-even $80 ÷ 10 = $8 per round trip. It cannot validate the rule, and not merely because the data are invented. Net R per trade is +1.95 (×4), −1.05 (×5) and −2.05; the sample SD is about 1.66R and the standard error about 0.53R, so the rough ±2 SE band (about −1.00R to +1.10R) includes zero. Dropping one winner makes the mean −0.16R, and the $8 break-even is only twice the assumed $4 cost. Ten trades with no comparator or independent window cannot validate a rule.

tasks.title: Allocate simultaneous candidates
tasks.question: A simplified Atlas-20 variant has equity E = $50,000, of which $12,000 is cash; its four held positions have risen since entry, so one slot is free. Use a $2 stop distance, a 0.5% price-risk allowance, a 10% notional cap measured at the limit price, and a cash allowance of (cash − $2.50 entry fee) ÷ limit. Eligible A: close 40.00, prior-20 high 39.00. Eligible B: close 20.40, prior-20 high 20.00. Rank by breakout margin, 100 × (close − prior-20 high) ÷ prior-20 high, rounded to 0.01 percentage point. Each limit is close × 1.01, rounded down to the cent. Which candidate gets the order, how many shares, and what cash reserve?
solution: A’s margin = 100 × (40.00 − 39.00) ÷ 39.00 = 2.5641…, which rounds to 2.56%; B’s = 100 × 0.40 ÷ 20.00 = 2.00%, so A ranks first. A’s limit = 40.00 × 1.01 = $40.40. Allowances: risk floor(0.5% × $50,000 ÷ $2) = floor(250 ÷ 2) = 125 shares; notional floor($5,000 ÷ $40.40) = 123; cash floor($11,997.50 ÷ $40.40) = 296. The smallest, 123, is the order, so the notional cap binds; planned 1R = 123 × $2 = $246, inside the $250 budget. Reserve 123 × $40.40 + $2.50 = $4,971.70, leaving $7,028.30 available. B stays eligible but gets no slot and is not re-offered later. Filled risk is fixed by the actual fill; there is no later substitution without a new decision.

tasks.title: Identify the research clock
tasks.question: A researcher logs six variants on 2015–19 data and locks one by a pre-written rule. Run once on held-out 2020–21 data, it averages +0.02R over 14 trades. After charting the held-out losers, she adds a filter: trade only if, within the prior 20 sessions, a completed low fell at least 1% below frozen range support and a later close within three sessions returned above it. On 2020–21 the filtered version earns +0.31R over 8 trades. (a) Label both results. (b) How many variants has the search now tried, and under Chapter 25’s independence model what is the chance that at least one no-edge variant passes a 5% test? (c) At which close is each filter event first known? (d) What data may evaluate the new version, and what must be frozen first?
solution: (a) The locked result, +0.02R over 14 trades, stays the held-out result for v1 as recorded. The filtered +0.31R is development evidence for a new version, v2, because the 2020–21 window shaped the filter; it is not a held-out test.

(b) Seven variants. If each were an independent 5% test of a rule with no edge, 1 − 0.95⁷ ≈ 0.302, about 30%; variants that share trades make the true figure different, but reporting only the survivor still overstates the evidence. (c) Each filter event is known only at the close that returns above support, not at the breach low; using it earlier is look-ahead. (d) Only a fresh window or a paper forward study. Before it starts, freeze the filter definition and its recognition time, the comparator (v1 on the same window), the cost model and the decision criteria.
